stem: A nurse compares the hemodynamic mechanisms of septic shock, anaphylactic shock, and neurogenic shock. Which characteristic is shared by all three?

options.A: Pathologic vasodilation with reduced systemic vascular resistance causing distributive shock
options.B: Primary loss of intravascular volume as the initiating cause of hypovolemic shock
options.C: Primary failure of myocardial contractility as the initiating cause of cardiogenic shock
options.D: Mechanical obstruction of blood flow as the initiating cause of obstructive shock

rationale: A is correct. Septic, anaphylactic, and neurogenic shock are forms of distributive shock. Although their triggers differ, each can produce pathologic vasodilation and reduced systemic vascular resistance, leading to maldistribution of blood flow and inadequate tissue perfusion. Sepsis and anaphylaxis can also involve increased capillary permeability, while neurogenic shock results from loss of sympathetic vascular tone. B, C, and D describe the primary mechanisms of hypovolemic, cardiogenic, and obstructive shock rather than the shared distributive mechanism.
educational_objective: Differentiate distributive shock from other shock categories by recognizing pathologic vasodilation and reduced systemic vascular resistance as a shared mechanism in septic, anaphylactic, and neurogenic shock.
source_organization: National Library of Medicine, National Center for Biotechnology Information
source_version_date: Last updated July 24, 2023; current NCBI chapter accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: Introduction; Etiology; Pathophysiology — distributive/vasodilatory shock involves systemic vasodilation; common etiologies include sepsis and anaphylaxis, with neurogenic shock in trauma; mechanisms include inflammatory/histamine-mediated vasodilation or loss of sympathetic vascular tone
source_claim_supported: Septic, anaphylactic, and neurogenic shock are distributive shock states that share pathologic vasodilation/reduced systemic vascular resistance, although sepsis and anaphylaxis may additionally involve capillary leak and neurogenic shock results from loss of sympathetic tone.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing

correction_summary: Rebuilt the source classification-recall item into a mechanism comparison. Removed the inaccurate implication that distributive shock necessarily occurs despite fully adequate circulating blood volume and instead tests the defensible shared feature—pathologic vasodilation with reduced systemic vascular resistance—while acknowledging capillary leak and etiologic differences.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: Verified against current NCBI/StatPearls Distributive Shock and corroborating NCBI shock references. The common mechanism is decreased vascular tone/systemic vasodilation; sepsis, anaphylaxis, and neurogenic shock are recognized distributive etiologies.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A is limited to the shared hemodynamic feature. The rationale explicitly avoids claiming identical causes or identical volume status across the three entities and notes the distinct capillary-leak versus sympathetic-loss mechanisms.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct. Reduced systemic vascular resistance from pathologic vasodilation is the shared distributive feature.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect. Primary intravascular volume loss defines hypovolemic shock and is not the shared initiating mechanism of all three conditions.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect. Primary pump failure defines cardiogenic shock, although myocardial dysfunction can coexist in sepsis.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect. Mechanical impedance to blood flow defines obstructive shock and is not the shared mechanism.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A applies across septic, anaphylactic, and neurogenic shock. Potential mixed physiology in individual patients does not change the primary classification tested.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are parallel hemodynamic mechanisms paired with a shock category and are comparable in length.
audit_findings.blueprint: Directly aligned with 2026 Physiological Adaptation pathophysiology and altered hemodynamics/tissue perfusion.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Re-audited for distributive-shock definition, systemic vascular resistance, capillary-leak nuance, septic cardiomyopathy overlap, relative versus absolute hypovolemia, classification ambiguity, and NCLEX relevance. No unresolved conflict remained.
